structure.title: Chapters 1–3 · Calculate before paying the price
structure.text: The opening chapters compare rulers, commanders, terrain, supplies and discipline before an army moves. A victory that empties the treasury or destroys the city one hoped to gain may look far less successful from the ruler's seat than from the battlefield.

structure.title: Chapters 4–8 · Arrange the encounter
structure.text: Position, concentration and surprise change the odds before opponents meet. The adversary's expectations enter the calculation as surely as the number of troops. A threatened point can make an enemy march where the commander wanted him to go.

structure.title: Chapters 9–13 · Read the ground and the people on it
structure.text: Dust, birds, roads, rivers and the distance from home can all carry intelligence. The final chapters bring fire and espionage into a book that repeatedly treats obtaining reliable knowledge as cheaper than sending an entire army to discover a fact too late.

people.name: The commander
people.role: A judge answerable for lives and resources
people.text: Courage is only one quality in the reckoning. A commander who can be provoked, flattered or embarrassed into fighting has allowed the enemy a share in the decision about when to commit the troops.

people.name: The adversary
people.role: An observer who can also be misled
people.text: Concealment and feints work because the other commander is drawing inferences too. Advice about deceiving an enemy often has a mirror image in advice about checking what one's own scouts believe they have seen.

context.title: The compact sayings share a problem
context.text: A maxim can sound universally applicable when detached from the adjacent discussion of supplies, roads or morale. The tactical situation usually identifies whose choice the author is analysing and what that person can afford to lose.

notice.text: Notice how a long supply line changes the value of food.
notice.why: The same sack of grain has very different costs depending on how far an army hauled it. Apparent digressions into accounts measure how much campaigning can be sustained before any battle is won.

notice.text: Read a sign in more than one direction.
notice.why: Disorder may reveal weakness or be displayed to invite attack. The very intelligence that promises an advantage can make its interpreter vulnerable to someone who knows what sign the observer is hoping to see.

opening: An army can win its battles and ruin the country that pays for them. Sun Tzu starts from the cost of fighting: exhausted soldiers, emptied stores, and decisions that become harder to reverse with every mile. His commander must understand terrain, deception, morale, and the enemy well enough to avoid depending on courage alone. These spare instructions give intelligence a ruthless practical purpose. The finest victory leaves little for a heroic story because the opponent's position has collapsed before the fighting begins.
